newsitem.title: INDIA: Sonia remains India's enigma in political debut.
newsitem.headline: Sonia remains India's enigma in political debut.

text.p: Sonia Gandhi was nowhere to be seen on the day she made her biggest political statement.

Her characteristic absence from the limelight on Thursday, when her entry into the Congress party was announced, underlined both her strengths and potential weaknesses as the embodiment of India's Nehru-Gandhi dynasty.

She has never wielded influence from centre stage, always from the wings where her carefully-groomed mystique is greatest and least vulnerable to the slings and arrows of politics. No one knows if her power can survive a public coming-out.
There was no fanfare in the white bungalow housing Congress headquarters on a leafy New Delhi street. Neither the 50-year-old Italian-born widow nor her spokesman could be reached.
The usually loquacious president of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), L.K. Advani, was tongue-tied and had no comment on her decision to enter the political fray.
Other groups, including Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's United Front coalition, were also studiously silent.

The low-key reception partly reflected the aura of uncertainty that has surrounded Sonia Gandhi since her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, was blown up by a suicide bomber while campaigning for general elections in 1991, analysts said.
The parties' reactions could be explained by their ambivalence towards an enigmatic figure whose ultimate political impact could be slim or great -- nobody knows.

"Sonia's formal entry into the Congress at this stage is likely to destabilise the established leadership of the party, upset the fragile understanding between the Congress and the United Front...and give a new issue to the BJP to flog," the Indian Express said.
But Charan Wadhwa of the Centre for Policy Research said: "I would not read too much into this."
For many in Congress, Sonia, as she is known in India, is the extension of the powerful dynasty which has controlled both the party and India for 38 of its 50 years since independence.

"Of course, there is an immediate gain for the Congress," the Pioneer newspaper said. "With Mrs Gandhi making a formal entry into the political arena, the party may once again be able to exhibit a semblance of unity."
But she is also part of the bitter infighting which has helped to push Congress to the sidelines of power after decades of smug dominance.
"This means she will be drawn more directly into the factional struggles," said B.G. Verghese of the Centre for Policy Research.

Congress president Sitaram Kesri lauded Sonia Gandhi's decision to take the modest plunge into politics, but he did not trumpet her arrival as he had done when some other well-known personalities joined the party.

"In the short run, Kesri will gain by Sonia's entry," said Mahesh Rangarajan of the Centre for Contemporary Studies. "But the next logical step would be for her to become party leader. That would not be good for Kesri."

Still, Sonia's first political step was a very modest one. She joined Congress as a "primary" member, stopping short of joining the party's "active" roll which is a prerequisite for a leadership post.
For some of Congress's rivals, Sonia represents a potential galvanising force that could alter the balance of power in the world's most populous democracy.
"The bad news is that over a period of time, Congress could become stronger and it could lead to more political uncertainty for some months ahead," a Bombay-based broker said.
"This is bound to cause tremors in the United Front," said the Pioneer newspaper.

But some commentators predicted that untested Sonia would remain on the fringes and never play a public leadership role that could draw her into the vortex of power where her husband and mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, lost their lives.
"She is a much more potent figure on the outside," Verghese said. "The moment she enters the fray, she will be chewed up."
